The Highland Loop: Scotland's Greatest Motorcycle Circuit

This 7-day loop from Inverness takes in the very best of the Scottish Highlands — Glen Coe, the Isle of Skye, Torridon, Applecross, and sections of the NC500. It's a concentrated dose of Highland magic that covers approximately 800 miles of the most spectacular roads in Britain.

Day 1: Inverness to Fort William (130 miles)

Head south via the A82 along Loch Ness to Fort Augustus, then continue through the Great Glen to Fort William. The road follows the Caledonian Canal and passes through increasingly dramatic scenery. Ben Nevis, Britain's highest mountain, looms over Fort William. Stay in the town and prepare for tomorrow's highlight.

Day 2: Fort William to Skye (100 miles)

Ride the A82 through Glen Coe — Britain's most dramatic valley. The Three Sisters loom overhead as you ride through the glacial pass. Continue north to Glen Garry, then west on the A87 through Glen Shiel (Five Sisters of Kintail) to the Skye Bridge. Arrive on Skye with the rest of the day to explore.

Day 3: Isle of Skye (80 miles)

A full day on Skye. Ride to the Quiraing in the north, the Fairy Pools at Glen Brittle, and Neist Point lighthouse. The island's roads are varied — from flowing A-roads to narrow single-track. The scenery is otherworldly: jagged peaks, sea cliffs, and ever-changing light.

Day 4: Skye to Applecross (90 miles)

Leave Skye via the Skye Bridge and head south to Loch Carron. From Kishorn, tackle the Bealach na Bà — Britain's greatest road pass. Arrive in Applecross and celebrate with local seafood and a pint at the Applecross Inn.

The Highland Loop builds perfectly — each day is better than the last. By day 4, when you crest the Bealach na Bà, the Highlands have you completely.

Day 5: Applecross to Ullapool (80 miles)

Coast road north from Applecross to Shieldaig, then through Torridon and past the extraordinary mountains of Liathach and Beinn Eighe. Continue north through Gairloch to Ullapool. This is remote, empty, stunning riding.

Day 6: Ullapool to Durness (100 miles)

Follow the NC500 north through Lochinver past Suilven and Stac Pollaidh. The landscape becomes increasingly wild and Scandinavian. Arrive at Durness on the north coast — the most northwesterly point of mainland Britain.

Day 7: Durness to Inverness (120 miles)

The north coast road east to Tongue, then south through Lairg back to Inverness. A fitting final day through empty Highland country, with the route gradually softening as you approach the capital of the Highlands.

Essential Planning

  • Best season: Late May to mid-September. Midges are worst June-August
  • Accommodation: Book all accommodation in advance — this route covers popular areas with limited beds
  • Fuel: Fill up at every opportunity on the west coast. Stations can be 50+ miles apart
  • Weather: Pack for all conditions. The west coast sees significant rainfall
keyTakeaways: A 7-day, roughly 800-mile loop from Inverness taking in Glen Coe, Skye, Torridon, Applecross and NC500 sections.
The route builds day by day, peaking at the Bealach na Ba on day four into Applecross.
Day three is a full day exploring Skye, from the Quiraing to the Fairy Pools and Neist Point.
Best ridden late May to mid-September; midges are worst June to August.
Book all accommodation ahead and fill up at every opportunity on the west coast.

faq.q: How long is the Highland loop?
faq.a: It is a 7-day circuit of roughly 800 miles starting and finishing in Inverness. It concentrates the very best of the Highlands, including Glen Coe, the Isle of Skye, Torridon, Applecross and sections of the NC500, into one route. The stages range from an 80-mile day on Skye to a 130-mile opening run down Loch Ness to Fort William.

faq.q: What is the highlight of the route?
faq.a: Day four's Bealach na Ba into Applecross is the crescendo. This former drovers' pass climbs from sea level to 626 metres in a sequence of tight, committing hairpins that feel more Alpine than Scottish. The route deliberately builds towards it, and the Applecross Inn at the foot of the descent rewards you with fresh seafood and a view over the bay.

Late May to mid-September offers the best weather and daylight. Midges are at their worst from June to August, so late May and September are the sweet spots for dodging both bugs and the heaviest coach traffic. The west coast sees significant rainfall in any month, so pack for all conditions regardless of the forecast.

Fill up at every opportunity on the west coast, where stations can be 50 miles or more apart and some keep short hours. The far north-west around Assynt and Sutherland is especially remote. Treat a half-full tank as your cue to refuel rather than gambling on the next station being open, particularly on the Torridon and Ullapool legs.

faq.q: Do I need to book accommodation in advance?
faq.a: Yes. This route covers popular areas with limited beds, so book every night ahead, especially on Skye and in Applecross, Ullapool and Durness. Turning up hoping for a room in peak season is risky. Planning your overnights also lets you pace the days sensibly, as the mileage always takes longer than it looks on these roads.
